source.title: Rolling the dice for better deep learning performance: A study of randomness techniques in deep neural networks
source.authors: Mohammed Ghaith Altarabichi; Sławomir Nowaczyk; Sepideh Pashami; P. Mashhadi; Julia Handl

record.tranche_reason: Ablates optimizer and dropout choices and reports held-out test performance, using a different method and a joint hyperparameter search rather than the claim versions' specified comparisons.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-accuracy ablations for optimizer and dropout, which bear on V4 and V6. Its batch-size discussion concerns optimizer preferences and training instability; it does not report a large-versus-small-batch held-out performance comparison under a fixed epoch budget. Random-label memorization, width sweeps, convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparisons for generalization, sharpness measures, and removal of memorized examples were not tested. Hyperparameter selections and cited prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: Test-accuracy comparisons and ablations bear on V3, V4 and V6 under joint hyperparameter optimization. The study does not reproduce the original protocols.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors recommend vanilla SGD for highest accuracy on harder datasets, momentum SGD for large batches, and Adam when tuning resources are limited. They report that DropConnect performs better in fully connected settings and dropout in convolutional settings; the experiments do not isolate individual layer types.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses PSO to jointly tune 22 randomness mechanisms, then ablates selected configurations on FC and VGG-like CNNs across four image datasets. It does not reproduce the original methods specified in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer, architecture, and dataset affect the reported results. The authors also report SGD training instability with batch sizes larger than 512, but do not give a matched held-out performance comparison by batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing other optimizers with SGD caused training instability at batch sizes above 512.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer substitution can destabilize training when the remaining recipe uses large batches.

record.problems: The authors state that conclusions are conditioned on standard architectures and low-resolution, “easy” datasets, and that more datasets and architectures would strengthen them. Results relevant to optimizer choice are mainly qualitative or selection frequencies rather than per-optimizer test-accuracy comparisons. The dropout result across CNN settings is aggregated across four datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible additional rows identified. Hyperparameter selection frequencies beyond optimizer choice, cited prior work, and training-curve comparisons for the paper's proposed loss noise and gradient dropout were excluded because they do not test the mapped claim versions.

untested.parts: Own experiments comparing random-label memorization with natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and training to convergence.
The contribution of local connectivity, learned sparse connectivity, convolutional initialization of fully connected networks, and comparisons matched for parameter count.

Learning-rate-and-decay-only tuning, controlled comparisons of narrow versus broad tuning budgets, matched training performance, language benchmarks, decoupled weight decay, and Adam-to-SGD switching.
Held-out comparisons across identified batch sizes under a fixed epoch budget and tests of the specified compensating recipes.
Very small training sets, excessive-dropout underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Memorization-based example removal and retraining against random-removal controls.

missing.what: FC/MNIST individual-dropout comparison: median test accuracy 97.66% versus default 97.34%, with 12.03% error reduction, over five independent runs. The selected dropout rate and significance are not recoverable from the supplied table formatting.
missing.locator: Table 3, Single-Technique Search, Dropout and Default settings

missing.what: MNIST architecture comparison: default CNN accuracy 99.42% versus FC 97.34%; optimized CNN configurations reach 99.60–99.69% versus FC 98.37–98.54%. Architecture and parameter count differ, so these results cannot isolate local connectivity.

The authors explicitly report that Adam generalizes worse than the SGD family, especially on harder datasets. Record this as a qualitative finding with no reported effect size, rather than treating optimizer selection counts as performance measurements.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Optimizer ablations retain hyperparameters selected jointly with the original optimizer, limiting conclusions about independently tuned alternatives. Figure-only values cannot be reconstructed from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or held-out comparison between natural and random labels.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
FC and CNN are evaluated, but the study does not report a controlled comparison of their generalization or test local connectivity.

Tests optimizer choice in its configurations and ablations, but not the specified image and language benchmark comparison under limited learning-rate and decay-schedule tuning, broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, or Adam-to-SGD switching.
Does not compare held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets or test the listed recipe adaptations.
Tests dropout's ablation contribution in its FC and CNN settings, but not the specified very-small-training-set regime or joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap measure.
No removal and retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: FC network
rows.size_stated: Two hidden layers of fifty neurons each.
rows.operation_detail: Ablation replaced the selected Adam optimizer with Vanilla SGD; authors report training instability, particularly with large batch sizes.

conditions.value: particularly large; exact values not stated

rows.measure: Test-performance contribution of optimizer ablation; qualitative report of training instability
rows.baseline: Optimized setting with selected optimizer (Adam in four of five runs)
rows.value: Replacing Adam with Vanilla SGD resulted in training instabilities
rows.uncertainty: Positive ERR median over the five settings was reported as statistically significant at 0.05; no uncertainty for this optimizer-specific statement.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Experiment II - the ablation study; Fig. 2
rows.note: This is an optimizer ablation in the FC/MNIST search, not a broad matched comparison of adaptive methods with SGD.
rows.check: The row emphasizes training instability, which alone cannot establish generalization. Add the reported test-ERR result: optimizer choice was the largest contributor and had a significantly positive median across five FC settings; Adam was selected in four. This favors the selected optimizer over default SGD under unchanged accompanying hyperparameters, without establishing superiority over separately tuned SGD. The significance statement applies to the aggregate optimizer ablation.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Reported optimizer selection frequency across the optimized settings.
rows.measure: Optimizer selection frequency; authors also state Adam generalization performance falls short compared with the SGD family, especially on more challenging datasets.
rows.value: Adam was successful in 4 settings with the easier datasets MNIST and Fashion MNIST; SGD with Momentum was chosen in 8 instances; Vanilla SGD was selected 7 times out of 10 for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.
rows.locator: Section 5.4, Which optimizer to choose?; Section 6, Conclusions
rows.note: Frequency and qualitative generalization conclusion are reported; per-optimizer test accuracy values are not given here.
rows.check: Optimizer selection frequencies should not be result rows: they do not measure a held-out performance difference between optimizers. Separate the authors' qualitative generalization finding from these frequencies; no per-optimizer accuracy difference or statistical test is supplied.

rows.subject: FC network
rows.size_stated: Two hidden layers of fifty neurons each.
rows.operation_detail: Ablation removed the selected dropout setting by setting its decision variable to the default.
rows.measure: Positive error-rate-reduction contribution from dropout ablation
rows.baseline: Optimized setting with selected randomness configuration
rows.value: Dropout offered a positive ERR contribution only once
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Experiment II - the ablation study; Fig. 2
rows.note: The paper calls dropout's performance poor in this FC setting.
rows.check: Positive contribution in only one of five settings supports an inconsistent benefit. The other four are not separately identified as zero versus negative, and their selected dropout rates are unavailable.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Ablation measured the contribution of dropout in the optimized CNN settings.
rows.measure: Positive median ERR contribution; frequency of positive ERR contributions
rows.baseline: Optimized setting with selected randomness configuration
rows.value: Dropout had a positive median ERR over the 20 settings, statistically significant at 0.05; it contributed positively in 12 settings.
rows.uncertainty: Student’s t-test p-value threshold 0.05; exact p-value not stated
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Experiment II - the ablation study; Section 5.2; Fig. 5
rows.note: Results aggregate the 20 CNN settings across four datasets; dataset-specific dropout outcomes are not enumerated in the text.
rows.check: A significantly positive median test-ERR contribution establishes benefit in this pooled CNN regime; V6 does not require universal benefit. Retain the qualification that only 12 of 20 settings had positive contributions. Cite Section 4.2 and Fig. 3 for the significant median, and Section 5.2 and Fig. 5 for the count.
